amendments.rule: **A cognate infinitive absolute the ASV renders with a distinct adverbial word takes that word as its own unit.** The finite cognate verb retains its subject, auxiliaries and lexical verb phrase under rule 17, while the infinitive absolute takes the English word spent on its emphasis and heads on that word: `פָּקֹד יִפְקֹד` → *will surely visit* gives *surely* to the infinitive absolute and *will visit* to the finite verb, and `הָשֵׁב יָשִׁיב` → *will fully requite* gives *fully* and *will requite* on the same terms. This is rule 2's smallest defensible unit rather than rule 30 fusion, because the ASV has written a separate English word for the infinitive absolute's contribution. The finished corpus has 34 Qal infinitive-absolute units across 26 chapters independently aligned to *surely*, *utterly*, *indeed*, *diligently* or *certainly*, all headed on the intensifier. **Read that word as whatever the ASV has spent on the emphasis, and not as a class of intensifying adverbs.** Where the clause is a rhetorical, concessive or conditional one and the ASV writes a minimizing or restrictive adverb in that same slot, the word is the infinitive absolute's on exactly the same terms and heads its unit: `וְאָבִיהָ יָרֹק יָרַק בְּפָנֶיהָ` → *If her father had* ***but*** *spit in her face* gives *but* to the infinitive absolute and *had spit* to the finite verb. **And read *word* as one English rendering rather than one English token, exactly as rule 30 reads its own one-word condition.** Where the ASV spends a fixed multi-word adverbial expression on that emphasis, the whole expression is the infinitive absolute's one unit: no part of it is `added`, no part of it is a neighbouring morpheme's, and the unit heads under rules 24 and 31 on the content word the expression turns on rather than on one of its function words. `הֲיָכוֹל יָכְלוּ אֱלֹהֵי גּוֹיֵי הָאֲרָצוֹת` → *Were the gods of the nations of the lands* ***in any wise*** *able* gives *in any wise* to the infinitive absolute, headed on *wise*, while the finite verb keeps its bare *able* and the interrogative particle keeps the fronted copula rule 20 gives it; the *in* and the *any* state nothing on their own and no morpheme in the clause answers to either, so rule 15's supplied determiner and rule 11's function-word priority do not reach them. But read what stands in the clause before taking the whole expression: where a negative, a `כֹּל` or another morpheme is itself what a word of that expression says, that morpheme takes it under rules 35, 41 and 48 and the infinitive absolute takes only the rest. Test by subtraction as rules 16, 31 and 43 do: drop the English word and ask whether the infinitive absolute has lost its whole rendering or only the clause has lost a shade of force. Do not mark such a word `added` under rule 30 or fold it into the finite verb, into a conjunction or into a negative standing beside it, for the reason rule 42 gives about a surplus *and* and rule 51 about a supplied *also*: a morpheme stands in the clause for it, no other morpheme answers to it, and the word is written beside those renderings rather than inside one of them. Where the ASV writes no distinct adverbial word at all for the infinitive absolute, the ordinary rules decide what, if anything, realizes it. **And a finite auxiliary verb whose whole contribution the ASV writes as an adverb is read on exactly those terms.** Hebrew writes a second verb where English writes an adverb of repetition, continuation or degree — `שׁוּב` for *again*, `יָסַף` for *any more*, `רָבָה` hiphil for *much* — and where the ASV spends its English on that verb's contribution while another verb in the clause holds the lexical predicate, the auxiliary verb takes that word as its own unit and heads on it, exactly as an infinitive absolute takes the word spent on its emphasis. `וַיָּשָׁב וַיִּבֶן אֶת־הַבָּמוֹת` → *he built* ***again*** *the high places* gives *again* to `שׁוּב` and *he built* to `בָּנָה`; `לֹא אֹסִיף לְהָנִיד` → *neither will I cause ... to wander* ***any more*** gives *will I any more* to `יָסַף`, headed on *more*, and *cause ... to wander* to the infinitive; `הִרְבָּה לַעֲשׂוֹת הָרַע` → *he wrought* ***much*** *evil* gives *much* to `רָבָה`. The subject pronoun, the auxiliaries and the infinitive marker are placed as they otherwise would be by rules 17, 48 and 52 — on the auxiliary verb where it is the clause's finite verb and on the other verb where the ASV has made that one the English predicate — and the unit is discontinuous under rule 25 where the adverb stands apart from them. Do not mark such an adverb `added`, and do not fold it into the lexical verb's unit as a phrasal particle under rule 44: what that rule's surplus-particle sentence governs is a word no morpheme licenses, and here a written verb is what the word renders, which the subtraction test rules 16, 31 and 43 use finds gone with it while the lexical verb keeps its whole rendering either way. Read the source verbs against the English words, as rule 42 counts waws against *and*s: where the ASV writes a verb for each — *returned and built* — rule 2 splits them and each takes its own, and where it writes nothing at all for the auxiliary verb the ordinary rules decide what, if anything, realizes it. **And a connective the ASV leaves unwritten between two such verbs is counted as rule 14 directs.** Hebrew coordinates the pair with a waw that English does not write, so where two conjunctions stand and the ASV writes one connective, the surplus waw is `unrepresented`; do not fold it into either verb's unit to avoid the mark.
amendments.why: 2KI.21 met the same construction four times — `שׁוּב` → *again* (v3), `יָסַף` → *any more* (v8), `רָבָה` → *much* (vv. 6 and 16) — a finite verb whose entire contribution the ASV writes as an adverb while a different verb holds the lexical predicate. Rule 56 already governs exactly that shape for the infinitive absolute, so the qualification belongs in its text rather than in a new rule pointing back at it. Without it, rule 44's surplus-particle sentence points the other way: a pass reading *he built again* against `בָּנָה` alone would find *built* already writing the whole lexeme and mark *again* `added`, leaving the written `שׁוּב` unrendered against rule 2. Nothing in the contract or the precedent above contradicts the reading, and rule 30's own test excludes the only other candidate analysis — fusing the two verbs into one unit — because `בָּנָה` owns *built* outright. The closing sentence records the waw count the same chapter forced at v3, where two conjunctions stand under a single written *For*.

conventions: The regnal age formula `בֶּן X שָׁנָה` (2KI.21.1, 2KI.21.19): the construct `בֵּן` is the predicate of the verbless clause and carries the ASV's *was ... old*, discontinuous under rule 25 around the numeral and its counted noun, which keep their own words; the copula joins that predicate under rule 20. Do not mark `בֵּן` unrepresented, and do not leave *old* to the numeral or to the counted noun.

The succession formula `תַּחְתָּיו` → *in his stead* (2KI.21.18, 2KI.21.24, 2KI.21.26): the preposition takes *in ... stead* as one compound rendering, discontinuous under rule 25 around the possessive, and the suffix takes *his* under rule 18. The unit heads on *stead*, which carries the relation.

`כָּעַס` hiphil → *provoke to anger*, *provoked to anger* (2KI.21.6, 2KI.21.15) heads on the verb rather than on *anger*: the ASV never writes *provoke* alone for this lexeme, so *to anger* is what English spends on the relation and not a complement the verb lacks. Both units name the competing rule 44 reading, which heads on the complement. A supplied object pronoun standing inside that frame is `added` where the Hebrew writes no object morpheme, as at 2KI.21.6, and belongs to the suffix where one is written, as at 2KI.21.15.

The formula `הָרַע בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה` (2KI.21.2, 9, 15, 16, 20): the substantival article takes *that which* headed on the pronoun under rule 41, the adjective takes the construction-supplied copula with *evil*, `עַיִן` takes a supplied *the sight* under rule 29 and the divine name takes *of Jehovah* under rule 19. Where the ASV instead renders the adjective attributively — *much evil* at 2KI.21.6 — no determiner stands before the adjective's word, so the article is `unrepresented` under rule 29 and the adjective keeps the bare *evil*.

A two-morpheme subordinating pair rendered by a single English word is recorded `aligned` under rule 30 and headed on the governing first morpheme under rule 23, not `noncompositional`: `כַּאֲשֶׁר` → *as* (2KI.21.3, 13, 20), `יַעַן אֲשֶׁר` → *because* (2KI.21.11, 15), `עַד אֲשֶׁר` → *till* (2KI.21.16). The corpus writes `כַּאֲשֶׁר` → *as* both ways — 264 units `aligned` against 109 `noncompositional` — and this chapter takes the `aligned` reading throughout, since rule 6 reaches a genuinely indivisible phrase and rule 2 prefers the split wherever a defensible source head is available.

report: Read the 43-lemma candidate table, the four `added` units (which that table cannot see), and all 26 verses end to end. No cross-verse split found, so patches is empty.

Substantival `הָרַע` (vv. 2, 9, 15, 16, 20) beside attributive `much evil` (v6) is rule 29's determiner count and not a split: five verses write `that which` for the article, v6 writes no determiner for it at all and the article is unrepresented.

Article fronting agrees with itself in both directions: fronted onto the article where the rectum is anarthrous (`צְבָא הַשָּׁמַיִם` -> the host of heaven, vv. 3, 5), not fronted where the ASV renders the rectum arthrously and writes a `the` for each word (`עַם־הָאָרֶץ` -> the people of the land, v24).

Preposition plus `פָּנֶה` fuses uniformly and always heads on the construct noun -- `מִפְּנֵי` -> before (vv. 2, 9), `לְפָנָיו` -> were before (v11), `עַל־פָּנֶיהָ` -> upside down (v13) -- and in both suffixed cases the suffix stays outside the fusion with the pronoun the ASV wrote, as rule 30 directs.

The two supplied pronouns of v13 differ on source grounds and not by English parallelism: `מָחָה` writes no pronominal morpheme, so the `it` of `wiping it` is `added`, while `עַל־פָּנֶיהָ` writes a 3fs suffix denoting the dish, which takes the `it` of `turning it`. That is the right way round, since rule 30 reserves `added` for English no morpheme licenses.

The remaining multi-treatment lemmas track what the ASV wrote: `whereof` (v4) and `of which` (v7) both go whole to the relative; `לְ` is decided by whether a function word is written; `did` at v9 is a pro-verb for the gapped infinitive under rule 34 while `did` at v3 and v20 is a written verb; `more than` (v9) and `above` (v11) are one comparative `מִן` rendered two ways.

BSB: no genuine error. The `לְ` x7, `Td` x8 and object-marker rows are the documented convention difference (rules 16, 21, 27, 40, 41, 47). The one lexical item, the v3 waw, is forced -- two conjunctions stand there and the ASV writes a single `For`, so one waw is unrepresented whichever one takes the word.

The two flagged review items hold up. The three-morpheme `לְבַד מִן` -> besides (v16) is contiguous, one English rendering, no morpheme owning a part of it, so rule 30's condition is met. The `וְגַם` -> Moreover fusion (v16) rests on rule 22's closing paragraph, and its note names the competing reading that gives the word to the waw alone.

Recorded five conventions and one amendment. The amendment is to rule 56: this chapter met a finite auxiliary verb rendered as an adverb four times (`שׁוּב` -> again v3, `יָסַף` -> any more v8, `רָבָה` -> much vv. 6, 16), which rule 56 already governs in the infinitive-absolute shape while rule 44's surplus-particle sentence invites the wrong answer.
